summary: An FYI document containing biographical information about members of the IAB, the IESG, and the IRSG. It is informational and gives a picture of the people leading Internet standards at the time.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a snapshot of the people who steered the Internet's standards work in 1992. It holds one short biography for each member of the Internet Activities Board, the Internet Engineering Steering Group and the Internet Research Steering Group, written by the people themselves.

subtitle: Biographies of the people who led the Internet standards work in 1992, collected in one FYI memo.

tldr.problem: The Internet was built and standardised by volunteers whose names appeared nowhere useful, and the people running the standards bodies were invisible to the users of the network.
tldr.mechanism: The author sent a request to every member of the IAB, the IESG and the IRSG asking for a three paragraph biography, and compiled the replies unchanged into an FYI RFC.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1336 is an Informational FYI memo from May 1992 that obsoleted RFC 1251. It documents the people in office at the time and has not been obsoleted since.

today: RFC 1336 is an Informational FYI memo published in May 1992 that obsoleted RFC 1251. It has not been obsoleted since, and it stands as a record of who held the Internet's standards posts at that time.

sections.title: Why This Document Exists
sections.content:
There are thousands of networks in the Internet, tens of thousands of host machines and hundreds of thousands of users. It takes a great deal of effort to manage the resources and protocols that make the Internet possible. Sites may have people who are paid to manage their hardware and software, but the infrastructure of the Internet is managed by volunteers who spend considerable portions of their valued time to keep people connected.

Hundreds of people attend the three IETF meetings each year, representing government, the military, research institutions, educational institutions and vendors from all over the world. Most of them are volunteers who attend to learn and to contribute what they know. A few people deserve special notice: those who sit on the IAB, the IESG and the IRSG. Not only do they spend time at the meetings, they spend additional time organizing them, and they are the IETF's interface to other standards bodies and to the funding institutions. Without them, the IETF, and indeed the whole Internet, would not be possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet was run by volunteers, and the volunteers who organized the standards meetings were invisible to the people using the network. This memo puts their names and their own words on the record.

sections.title: How the Biographies Were Collected
sections.content:
In mid-February 1991 the author sent the following message to the members of the IAB, the IESG and the IRSG, and the responses are what the memo compiles.

The message began: the ARPANET is 20 years old, the next meeting of the IETF in St. Louis would be the 20th plenary, and it was a good time to credit the people who help make the Internet possible. The author explained that for now inclusion was limited to the members of those three groups, but that at some future time he would like to expand the number of people included.

He asked each of them to submit a biography in three paragraphs, for consistency: the first paragraph to contain the biography, the second the school affiliation and other interests, and the third the person's opinion of how the Internet has grown. He added that if there was anything else they would like to say, they were free to say it, because the object was to let the very large user community know about the people who give them what they have.
sections.plainLanguage: Every biography was written by the person it describes, to a fixed three-part shape: who they are, where they work and what they do, and their view of how the Internet has grown.

sections.title: The People Covered
sections.content:
The memo covers three bodies. The Internet Activities Board, or IAB, is the group that oversees the Internet's technical architecture. The Internet Engineering Steering Group, or IESG, is the steering group of the Internet Engineering Task Force, the IETF. The Internet Research Steering Group, or IRSG, is the steering group of the Internet Research Task Force, the IRTF.

The biographies are in alphabetical order and cover 24 people, each listed with the role they held: Philip Almquist, IETF Internet Area Co-director; Robert Braden, IAB Executive Director and IRSG member; Hans-Werner Braun, IAB member; Ross Callon; Vinton Cerf; Noel Chiappa; A. Lyman Chapin; David Clark; Stephen Crocker; James R. Davin; Deborah Estrin; Russell Hobby; Christian Huitema; Erik Huizer; Stephen Kent; Anthony G. Lauck; Barry Leiner; Daniel C. Lynch; David M. Piscitello; Jonathan B. Postel; Joyce K. Reynolds; Michael Schwartz; Bernhard Stockman; and Gregory Vaudreuil.

The memo states that the contents have not been edited and that only the formatting has been changed.
sections.plainLanguage: The 24 biographies cover the three groups that steer Internet standards and research, and each name is given with the office it held at the time.

sections.title: What a Biography Contains
sections.content:
Each entry follows the same shape, and the differences between them are what makes the document worth reading. Philip Almquist's entry describes an independent consultant in San Francisco, best known as the network designer for INTEROP '88 and INTEROP '89, who started at Carnegie-Mellon University in 1980 and moved to Stanford in 1983, where as the university's first hostmaster he invented Stanford's distributed host registration system and led its deployment of the Domain Name System.

Robert Braden's entry describes joining the networking research group at ISI in 1986, coming from UCLA where he had worked 16 of the preceding 18 years and had technical responsibility for attaching the first supercomputer to the ARPAnet in 1970. His closing paragraphs are his opinion on how the Internet has grown: he argues that collaboration proved more powerful than competition among researchers, warns that the prevailing mode may be shifting towards competition, both commercial and academic, and describes the scaling problems the IAB had been aware of since 1982.
sections.plainLanguage: The entries mix a career history with a personal view of how the Internet has changed, which is why the memo reads more like a set of interviews than a directory.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section of the memo is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. That is consistent with what the document is, a collection of biographies rather than a specification.
sections.plainLanguage: There is nothing about security here, because the document only describes people rather than protocols.

data.title: The message sent to the members
data.code:
The ARPANET is 20 years old.  The next meeting of the IETF in St.
Louis this coming March will be the 20th plenary.  It is a good
time to credit the people who help make the Internet possible.

I would like to ask you to submit to me your biography.  I intend
to compile the bios submitted into an FYI RFC to be published
before the next IETF meeting.  In order to maintain some
consistency, I would like to have the bios contain three
paragraphs.  The first paragraph should contain your bio, second
should be your school affiliation & other interests, and the third
should contain your opinion of how the Internet has grown.
